name: Hermeticism
era: 1st to 3rd century CE, revived from the 15th century
line: Look for the pattern, watch the mind and work the slow stages.

quote.text: That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to do the miracles of one only thing.
quote.source: Tabula Smaragdina, trans. after Isaac Newton’s manuscript version

quotes.text: A great wonder, Asclepius, is the human being.
quotes.source: Hermetic dialogue, Latin text, 3rd to 4th century CE

quotes.text: Unless you make yourself equal to God, you cannot understand God; like is understood by like.
quotes.source: Corpus Hermeticum XI, trans. after Brian Copenhaver

quotes.text: All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison.

words.meaning: Hermes the Thrice-Greatest; the legendary author of the Hermetica
words.usage: A figure who joined the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, honoured as a teacher of wisdom.

words.meaning: The writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus

words.meaning: The first treatise of the Corpus; often read as "shepherd of men"
words.usage: A vision in which Mind reveals the origin of the cosmos and the soul’s ascent.

words.meaning: A Hermetic dialogue surviving in Latin
words.usage: Known in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, with its famous praise of the human being.
In the Hermetica it is both a god and the divine part of a person.
The organising word or reason that shapes the cosmos.
In the Hermetica, knowledge of God and the self, rather than information.
The root of "cosmetic". The world seen as an ordered, beautiful whole.

words.meaning: The small world; a human being
words.usage: The idea that a person mirrors the larger cosmos.
The cosmos regarded as a living whole in which a person is a part.

words.meaning: The link between things at different levels
words.usage: The thought that a pattern repeats across scales.

words.meaning: First matter; the raw stuff of the work
words.usage: In alchemy, the basic material from which everything is made, and what the work begins with.
The long process of transformation. In alchemy it was the making of the philosophers’ stone.
The stage of dissolution and darkness.
The stage of washing and clarification.
A stage that was later often dropped from the sequence of colours.
The stage of completion.

The fifth element, beyond earth, water, air and fire.

The idea that the cosmos is a living being.
An alchemical motto for the repeated cycle of breaking down and making whole.
A short, cryptic text from the Arabic tradition, famed for the line "as above, so below".

words.usage: A practice of late antique philosophers. Not part of this Onda.
The subject of Corpus Hermeticum XIII, in which a student is "born again" in mind.

words.usage: The compulsion of planetary powers from which the Hermetic teaching promises release.
The idea that the parts of the cosmos influence each other.

words.meaning: A Paracelsian art of separating and recombining
words.usage: Coined by Paracelsus from words for "to separate" and "to join".

A modern text, not an ancient one. Its seven principles come from it.

practices.name: A page at dawn
practices.instructions: Read one short passage from a Hermetic text in a reliable translation, such as the opening vision of the Poimandres, in no more than a page. Read it slowly twice. Then close the book and sit for five minutes with one line in mind. Ask what it would mean if it were literally true and what it would mean as a figure of speech. Write one sentence of your own, not a summary.
practices.why: The Hermetic writings present themselves as teaching through vision and dialogue rather than argument. A short, slow reading each morning treats them as a way of thinking more than as a body of doctrine.
variations: Read the same page three days in a row.
Read it aloud to someone and ask what they hear.

practices.name: As above, so below
practices.instructions: Find one pattern that repeats at two scales: the branching of a river and of a tree, a spiral in a shell and in a galaxy picture, the rhythm of your breath and of the day. Look at both for a few minutes and draw the shared form. Then ask whether something in your own life repeats at a small and a large scale: a habit and a pattern of years. Write down the correspondence in one line.
practices.why: The Emerald Tablet’s famous line says that what is below is like what is above. Whatever the truth of cosmic claims, looking for the same pattern at different scales is a real way of seeing and a source of insight in science, craft and art.
variations: Look at a leaf with a magnifying glass and then at a satellite map.
Draw the pattern and give it a name.
Share the correspondence with a friend.

practices.name: Solve et coagula
practices.instructions: Choose one problem or confusion that is on your mind. First dissolve it: write down every part, doubt, fear and fact on a page, without ordering them. Leave it for a minute. Then bring it together: write a single sentence, or a short list, that says what the problem really is and the next small step. Name the stage you are in: blackening, whitening, yellowing or reddening.
practices.why: Alchemists described the work as a cycle of breaking down and making whole, passing through colour stages. Used as a metaphor for thinking and change, the cycle teaches that confusion is a stage and not a failure.
variations: Use it on a conflict with another person.
Use it on a piece of writing.
Keep a record of which stage you were in each night.

practices.name: Watching the mind
practices.instructions: Sit upright. Set a timer for ten minutes. Close your eyes or lower your gaze. Notice thoughts as they appear, as if you were watching them pass on a screen. Label them lightly: planning, remembering, worrying. Do not follow them or push them away. When you notice you have been carried off, return to watching. At the end ask: who was watching?
practices.why: In the Hermetic texts Mind, nous, is both a divine reality and the highest part of a person, and knowing oneself leads to knowing the whole. A simple practice of observing the mind gives that old idea a modern, practical form.
variations: Do it outdoors with your eyes open.
Count breaths from one to ten and begin again.
Write down the most frequent type of thought.

practices.name: One line of the Emerald Tablet
practices.instructions: Read one line of the Emerald Tablet in a translation you trust. Copy it out by hand. Write what it could mean in an ordinary day, then what it could mean at a larger scale (a city, the sky, a life). Note any doubt or disagreement without hurrying to resolve it.
practices.why: The Emerald Tablet is a short, famously obscure text that shaped centuries of alchemy and natural philosophy. Slow reading is the right speed for it.
variations: Draw the line as a diagram.

tasks.name: Write a laboratory-style notebook entry
tasks.meta: Date, weather, moon phase, what you observed

tasks.name: Look at the night sky and find one planet or the moon
Read one emblem from Atalanta Fugiens
Read one treatise of the Hermetica
Listen to The Planets with the night sky in mind
Journal: what pattern did you see at two scales today?
Write on “Mind and cosmos”: what in you mirrors what is outside?
Study one plate of Splendor Solis

rules.why: Renaissance and early modern alchemists were also experimenters. Check your claims against what you can observe.
Alchemical and scientific notebooks record observations. A record turns an impression into evidence.

rules.text: Look for the pattern beneath the surface
rules.why: The Hermetic habit is to ask what links things. Start with what repeats.
The word “hermetic” came to mean sealed and secret. Practise discretion: not everything you learn needs sharing.
The Great Work is long. Do not hurry the change you want, and notice which stage you are in.

rules.text: Never ingest or heat unknown substances
rules.why: This Onda uses alchemy as a symbol only. Mercury, arsenic and many old alchemical materials are poisons.

customs.title: Keep a notebook like a laboratory journal
customs.creator: Date, observation, result
customs.why: Early chemists and alchemists kept notebooks. Yours can hold observations, patterns and questions.

customs.title: Walk and notice patterns
customs.creator: A short walk in nature with attention to repeating forms

customs.title: Mark the days of the week as planetary names
customs.creator: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn
customs.why: English weekdays still carry the old planetary order. Treat it as symbol and history, not prediction.

customs.title: Spend an hour in silence
customs.creator: No talking, no media
customs.why: The Hermetic texts speak of silence as the condition of insight.

ethics.title: Knowledge as responsibility
ethics.text: In the Hermetica knowledge of the self and the cosmos is meant to change the one who knows. To know is to be obliged.
ethics.practice: Pick one thing you know and ask what it asks of you.

ethics.title: Self-mastery
ethics.text: The Poimandres describes the soul stripping away vices as it rises through the planetary spheres. The ideal is freedom from compulsion.
ethics.practice: Name one compulsion and delay it by ten minutes.

ethics.title: Discretion
ethics.text: The word hermetic means sealed. Teachings were passed carefully, to those prepared to receive them. Speaking less can be a form of respect.
ethics.practice: Keep one thing to yourself today, and notice what changes.

ethics.title: Reverence for nature
ethics.text: The Hermetic cosmos is alive and ordered, and the human being is its keystone. Care for the world follows from seeing it as a whole.
ethics.practice: Spend ten minutes caring for something living.

ethics.title: Honest experiment
ethics.text: Early alchemists, and later chemists, tried and recorded. Their best work depended on patience and honest reporting of failures.
ethics.practice: Record one failure from this week without excuses.

ethics.title: Humility before the whole
ethics.text: Hermetic thought sets a person in a vast web of connection. The one who sees the web cannot remain proud.
ethics.practice: Look at the stars for a few minutes and name your smallest worry.

philosophy.title: Mind and cosmos
philosophy.text: The Poimandres begins with a vision of Mind, who tells the seeker that the light is Mind, the same as the divine, and that the person is made of it. A person can know the whole because they share its nature.
philosophy.practice: Spend a moment aware of the awareness behind your thoughts.

philosophy.title: As above, so below
philosophy.text: The phrase comes from a line of the Emerald Tablet, a short text that came into Latin from Arabic in the Middle Ages. It states that the same pattern runs through every level of reality.
philosophy.practice: Look for one pattern at two scales today.

philosophy.title: The One and the All
philosophy.text: Hermetic texts and their Greek background favour the thought that all things are one, "hen to pan". The many things of the world are expressions of a single source.
philosophy.practice: Choose three unlike things you see today and ask what they share.

philosophy.title: Rebirth
philosophy.text: In Corpus Hermeticum XIII, Hermes teaches his son Tat a rebirth in which the vices are driven out and the powers of God enter. It is described as silent and inward.
philosophy.practice: Name one habit you are leaving behind, and write a line to mark it.

philosophy.title: The great wonder
philosophy.text: The Asclepius says that a human being is a great wonder, honoured and adored, because the person is both a mortal body and a divine mind. Pico della Mirandola quoted it in 1486 in his oration on human dignity.
philosophy.practice: Write down something about a human being that amazes you.

philosophy.title: The stages of the work
philosophy.text: Alchemical writers described a process that passed through colours: blackening, whitening, yellowing and reddening. They are taken as stages of change in matter and in the person.
philosophy.practice: Name the stage of a current project.

philosophy.title: Ascent through the spheres
philosophy.text: The Poimandres describes the soul rising through seven planetary spheres, leaving behind a vice at each, until it reaches the eighth and becomes divine. The picture is of a journey of release from compulsion.
philosophy.practice: List the "spheres" of your day and name one burden you could leave at each.

philosophy.title: A living world
philosophy.text: The idea of the anima mundi, a soul of the world, appears in Plato and in Renaissance Hermeticism. It sees nature as alive, not merely a machine.
philosophy.practice: Greet something non-human with attention, such as a tree.

philosophy.title: Silence
philosophy.text: In Corpus Hermeticum XIII the rebirth happens in silence. Whatever the doctrine, a good deal of understanding comes only in the quiet that follows talk.
philosophy.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes with no purpose.

philosophy.title: The modern seven principles
philosophy.text: The Kybalion, published in 1908, lists seven "Hermetic principles": mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. They are a modern synthesis, linked to New Thought, and not part of ancient Hermeticism.
philosophy.practice: If you meet the seven principles, ask where each one comes from before you accept it.

guide.origin: Greek-speaking Egypt, the Arabic world and Renaissance Europe
guide.era: 1st to 3rd century CE, revived from the 15th century
intro: Hermeticism is a tradition of writings and ideas gathered under the name of Hermes Trismegistus, "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest". The name joins the Greek god Hermes, the messenger and guide of souls, with the Egyptian god Thoth, patron of writing and wisdom. Greek-speaking writers in Egypt in the first centuries of the common era composed dialogues under this name, and later readers believed they were far older.

The core is the Corpus Hermeticum, seventeen Greek treatises, and the Latin Asclepius. They mix philosophy, cosmology and spiritual instruction. In the first, the Poimandres, a divine Mind reveals how the cosmos was made and how the soul, having fallen into matter, can rise back through the planetary spheres. Other treatises teach that the universe is alive and orderly, that a human being is a great wonder because both mortal and divine, and that knowledge of the self leads to knowledge of God. Separate "technical" Hermetica deal with astrology, alchemy and magic.

The texts passed into Arabic, where the Emerald Tablet and a large body of alchemical writing took shape, and into medieval Latin. In 1463 Marsilio Ficino, at the request of Cosimo de’ Medici in Florence, translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin from a Greek manuscript newly arrived from Macedonia. It was printed in 1471 and read across Europe. Many Renaissance thinkers, including Pico della Mirandola and Giordano Bruno, treated Hermes as an ancient Egyptian sage.

In 1614 the Swiss scholar Isaac Casaubon showed from the language that the texts were not ancient Egyptian but written in the early centuries CE. The finding changed the story but not the interest. The Hermetica remain important as a record of how people thought about mind, cosmos and the divine in late antiquity, and Hermetic ideas shaped alchemy, Renaissance natural philosophy and later occult movements.

Alchemy was not simply a failed attempt to make gold. Its practitioners were also physicians, metalworkers and philosophers who developed laboratory techniques and wrote about transformation in matter and in the person. Isaac Newton left a very large body of alchemical writing alongside his physics. The language of colours, stages and the Great Work offered a rich set of images for change.

Hermeticism today covers several things that should be kept apart: the ancient Hermetica, the Renaissance revival, historical alchemy, and modern esoteric movements such as the Golden Dawn and the authors of the Kybalion, published in 1908. This Onda draws mainly on the first two and treats alchemy as symbol and history. It offers attention, pattern-seeking and a slow method, and does not ask you to practise magic or handle chemicals.

figures.name: Hermes Trismegistus
figures.bio: The name under which the Hermetic texts were written. A blend of the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, honoured as a teacher in late antiquity and the Renaissance.

figures.name: Zosimos of Panopolis
figures.bio: A Greco-Egyptian alchemist and writer whose visions and technical works survive in fragments.

figures.name: Jabir ibn Hayyan
figures.bio: A name attached to a large Arabic corpus on alchemy. Scholars debate whether one person wrote it and who he was.

figures.name: Marsilio Ficino
figures.bio: Florentine philosopher who translated the Hermetica and Plato for Cosimo de’ Medici and shaped Renaissance Platonism.

figures.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
figures.bio: Italian humanist whose Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486, drew on the Hermetic praise of the human being.

figures.name: Paracelsus
figures.bio: Swiss physician and alchemist who sought chemical medicines and challenged the authority of ancient writers.

figures.name: John Dee
figures.bio: English mathematician, adviser to Elizabeth I and collector of books, who also pursued alchemy and angelic communication.

figures.name: Giordano Bruno
figures.bio: Italian philosopher who defended an infinite universe and was burned by the Roman Inquisition in 1600.

figures.name: Isaac Casaubon
figures.bio: Classical scholar who dated the Hermetica to the early centuries CE.

figures.name: Michael Maier
figures.bio: German physician and alchemist, author of Atalanta Fugiens.

figures.name: Isaac Newton
figures.bio: Mathematician and physicist who also wrote and collected a huge amount on alchemy and theology.

figures.name: Frances Yates
figures.bio: English historian whose book on Bruno and the Hermetic tradition, 1964, made the subject famous and remains debated.

history.when: c. 3rd century BCE to 2nd century CE
history.detail: In Hellenistic Egypt the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth were identified. Thoth, the god of writing and wisdom, was honoured at Hermopolis, called by the Greeks the city of Hermes.
Greek-speaking authors in Egypt composed the philosophical Hermetica, such as the Poimandres, and the technical Hermetica on astrology, alchemy and magic.
The alchemist wrote on the preparation of metals and recorded dream-like visions of transformation. He is one of the first named alchemists.
A Latin translation of a Greek Hermetic dialogue was made, and it reached medieval readers. It includes the praise of the human being and a controversial passage on animating statues.
In Baghdad and elsewhere translators rendered Greek works into Arabic, and the Emerald Tablet appeared in Arabic alchemical writings.
Robert of Chester translated an Arabic alchemical work in 1144, one of the first alchemical texts in Latin. The Emerald Tablet entered Latin soon after.
A Greek manuscript of the Corpus Hermeticum reached Florence around 1460. Ficino translated it by 1463, and it was printed in 1471.
Pico della Mirandola wrote his oration on the dignity of man, which quotes the Asclepius on the great wonder of the human being.
Isaac Casaubon showed from the Greek that the Hermetica were written in the early centuries CE and not in ancient Egypt, undermining the claim of great antiquity.
Michael Maier published a book of fifty emblems, verses and fugues on alchemy.
The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in London. It drew on Hermetic and other sources, and influenced twentieth-century occultism.
A book by "Three Initiates", often attributed to William Walker Atkinson, proposed seven Hermetic principles. It is a modern work.
Among the codices found in Egypt were three Hermetic treatises in Coptic, showing the texts were read in Egypt itself.
Brian Copenhaver’s English translation of the Hermetica made the texts accessible to scholars and general readers.

concepts.detail: In the Hermetica Mind is both a god, the source of the cosmos, and the highest part of a person. Knowing oneself as mind is the doorway to knowing God. It is less about thinking than about awareness.

concepts.text: The same pattern at every level.
concepts.detail: The line comes from the Emerald Tablet and is often used to summarise Hermetic thought. It suggests that a person, a society and the cosmos mirror each other. Used as a method, it asks you to look for structure that repeats.
Hermetic gnosis means knowing the divine and the self, not by inference but by insight. It transforms the knower. Many other late antique movements shared the word.

concepts.text: The person as a small world.
concepts.detail: Renaissance Hermeticism developed the idea that a human being contains the structure of the whole cosmos. Illustrations show the body mapped onto stars and planets. The symbol was used in medicine, art and philosophy.

Alchemists called their work the magnum opus. It involved stages of change in matter, often shown by colours, and the transformation of the practitioner. Later writers read it as a symbol of inner development.

Planets, metals, plants, organs and days of the week were thought to correspond. The system appears in astrology, medicine and magic. Modern readers can treat it as a structured set of symbols, not a set of facts.

concepts.text: The inward birth of the new person.
concepts.detail: Corpus Hermeticum XIII has Hermes initiate his son Tat into a rebirth, in which vices leave and divine powers enter. It is reached in silence and cannot be taught except by example.

concepts.text: A short, cryptic text on the unity of things.
concepts.detail: The Tabula Smaragdina first appears in Arabic works of the eighth or ninth centuries and was translated into Latin in the twelfth. Alchemists treated it as a summary of their art. Its language is deliberately obscure.

concepts.text: Fate, the rule of the planets.
concepts.detail: Many in late antiquity felt bound by the stars. The Hermetic texts promise freedom from this compulsion through knowledge, as the soul ascends and sheds each planetary vice.

concepts.text: The seven principles of the Kybalion.
concepts.detail: The 1908 Kybalion proposed seven principles: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. They reflect early twentieth-century New Thought, not ancient sources, and many popular claims about "Hermetic law" trace back to this book.

facts.text: The phrase "hermetically sealed" comes from alchemy: vessels were sealed with the "seal of Hermes", an airtight closure.
Ficino was told by Cosimo de’ Medici to translate the Hermetica before Plato, because Cosimo was old and eager to read it.
Isaac Casaubon redated the Hermetic writings in 1614, based on the Greek and the lack of any Egyptian influence in their language.
Atalanta Fugiens, published in 1617, includes fifty musical fugues for three voices alongside its emblems.
The Nag Hammadi library, found in 1945, contained Hermetic treatises in Coptic, including a prayer of thanksgiving.
Newton’s surviving papers include a very large quantity of writing on alchemy, much of it unpublished in his lifetime.
Paracelsus’s line that the dose makes the poison is still quoted in toxicology.

sensitivity.note: Hermeticism includes ancient philosophy, Renaissance learning, historical alchemy and modern esoteric movements. This Onda draws on the first two and treats alchemy as symbol and history. It offers habits of attention and does not ask you to practise ritual magic or handle chemicals.
requiredCaveats: Do not try to make or ingest any alchemical preparations. Many historical materials, such as mercury and arsenic compounds, are poisonous.
The Hermetica were written in the early centuries CE and not in ancient Egypt. The Kybalion and its seven principles are a modern text from 1908.
Astrological and planetary language here is symbolic and historical. It does not predict anything about your life, and nothing here is medical or financial advice.
